text: I now give the floor uh to his
excellency Boris Vaser Marjani Car
Guerrero, chair of delegation of Costa
Rica.
Mr. President,
>> with a great sense of humility and
respect, I address you and the
excellencies here in this illustrious
hall. More than eight decades ago, the
founders of the United Nations
understood that no peace built on brute
force could stand the test of time. They
opted instead for law, cooperation, and
dialogue as pillars of a new
international order.
Today, this conviction is facing one of
the toughest tests it has faced since
the organization's foundation. The world
stands in a period of deeprooted
fragmentation. The world is deeply
polarized. Armed conflicts are dragging
on longer than before. Transnational
organized crime is broadening its
capacity to act. Its tentacles are
growing longer. The effects of climate
change are growing ever more intense.
Development divides remain and the
technological transformation is posing
unprecedented challenges to our
institutions. At the same time, trust in
multilateralism
is waning precisely when we need it
most.
Standing before this landscape, Costa
Rica reaffirms its belief that no state,
no state can alone
address
challenges that are common to us all.
Multilateralism is a prerequisite for
the preservation of peace, to promote
sustainable development, and to protect
human dignity. However, multilateralism
will only preserve its dignity if it
proves able to yield tangible results,
specific results for people, for human
beings. Costa Rica
champions a United Nations which is more
agile, more efficient, more transparent
and
more accountable to its member states.
Our organization should establish
priorities, do away with overlaps, make
prudent use of its resources and measure
measure its results. President,
international peace and security are
facing increasingly complex threats.
Transnational organized crime, drug
trafficking, trafficking in persons,
weapons smuggling, asset laundering,
cyber crime and illegal mining transcend
national borders and undermine
democratic stability, development and
the rule of law.
Costa Rica has firsthand experience of
these threats. Illegal mining
spearheaded by transnational law organiz
transnational criminal organizations on
our border with Nicaragua has wrought
havoc on the environment and is
producing risks to public health, the
economy and regional security.
These organizations dispute territory.
They fuel illegal economies. They wage
attacks against democratic institutions
and directly affect the rights and
dignity of persons.
Artificial intelligence
can
boost cyber terrorism and other crimes
that we cannot yet envision. Costa Rica,
according to Microsoft system use data,
is the Latin American country that makes
greatest use of artificial intelligence.
We use it 58% more
than the other than the world on
average. These threats require greater
international cooperation, information
exchange, stronger institutions,
and a
renewed commitment to international law
and international humanitarian law. Mr.
President Costa Rica has demonstrated
that environmental leadership is not
measured by the size of a country's
territory, but rather by how unstinting
its commitment is to both present and
future generations. For decades, we have
championed a vision whereby economic
prosperity and the protection of nature
are not mutually exclusive goals.
Rather, they complement each other.
Climate change is dealing a particularly
heavy blow to the most vulnerable among
us. At the same time, biodiversity loss
is picking up pace, as is ecosystem
degradation, the pollution of our water
resources, and the pressures on our
oceans. These are not isolated
challenges.
They converge in one global crisis that
is imperiling food security, public
health and development opportunities for
millions and millions of people.
President, there can be no lasting
security
in a world where we see the erosion of
democratic institutions. There can be no
sustainable development when we violate
human rights. Our response must have
human beings at its heart. Costa Rica
will continue championing the dignity
and human rights of all persons, paying
particular attention to the inclusion,
autonomy, empowerment, and effective
participation of persons with
disabilities, including of persons
with autism. Against this backdrop, we
reiterate our grave concern at the
situation in Nicaragua. The erosion of
fundamental freedoms, the persecution of
dissenting voices, the shutdown of civic
space, religious persecution, and
reports of human rights violations
continue to draw the country further and
further away from democratic principles.
As a neighboring nation that has
welcomed hundreds and and hundreds of
thousands of Nicaraguan citizens, we
remain staunchly committed to defending
their rights and to the restoration of
the rule of law in Nicaragua. We also
note the situation in Cuba with concern
and we once again here appeal for the
full respect of human rights and
fundamental freedoms.
We also continue to closely follow
the situation in Venezuela as it
unfolds. We harbor the hope that
dialogue will prevail along with the
respect for the people's will, the
restoration of democratic institution
and the provision of care and services
to particularly vulnerable individuals.
President, 80 81 years after the
adoption of the charter, the best way to
defend the United Nations is to defend
its ability to discharge its mandates.
We need a UN which is more effective,
transparent, and agile, able to prevent
conflicts,
forge consensus even
in times of deeply rooted polarization.
We need a UN able to offer tangible
responses to the challenges of the 21st
century. For this reason, Costa Rica has
presented the candidacy of Miss Rebecca
Greenspan to the position of Secretary
General of the United Nations. She is a
Latin American women with woman with a
wealth of political economic experience
and experience in the multilateral
arena. She has a proven track record of
leadership. She knows the United Nations
from the inside and from outside and she
understands that knowing an institution
intimately and serving it also involves
having the courage to reform it. Her
candidacy is rooted in a simple but
powerful idea. Defending the United
Nations means and requires having the
courage to reform it. Today we need a
leader able to unite the membership,
strengthen the organization and renew
trust in international cooperation. We
need a UN
that does what it is called upon to do
in its founding charter that is maintain
international peace and security, ensure
respect for human rights and advance
development. Costa Rica firmly believes
that the next secretary general must be
a Latin American woman.
More than that, it must be Rebecca
Greenspan. Costa Rica abolished its army
more than seven decades ago. We did that
because we believed that international
law could offer greater security than
weapons.
I wish to repeat that Costa Rica
abolished its army more than seven
decades ago because it believed that
international law could offer greater
security than weapons. We will continue
to build bridges, crafting consensus and
defending the conviction that was the
very life force behind this
organization. That is that dialogue will
be more powerful than belligerance.
law will last longer than brute force
and cooperation is the only way that we
can achieve genuine lasting peace. The
future of the United Nations will not
depend solely on the strength of its
charter. Rather, it will depend upon our
collective courage to implement and
uphold that charter. To conclude,
President Excellencies one and all,
Costa Rica wishes peace, health, and
blessings to each and every one of you.
And we extend to you brotherly
greetings. That is you, the Costa Rican
people. Thank you.
>> I thank the chair of delegation of Costa
Rica.
